unit.name: The Empress by Tanika Gupta
unit.subtitle: Victorian Britain through Indian eyes: an ayah on the docks, an Indian MP at Westminster, and Queen Victoria's munshi.

lessons.title: Plot and Structure: Two Worlds, One Empire
lessons.content_html:
A Play of Two Worlds

Tanika Gupta’s The Empress spans two contrasting worlds that would never ordinarily appear on the same stage: the dockside poverty of Tilbury and the gilded interiors of Windsor Castle. The play opens in 1887, the year of Queen Victoria’s Golden Jubilee, and follows its threads across roughly a decade and a half of the late Victorian era. Its two-act structure holds two parallel storylines in tension throughout, intercutting between them so that the audience builds understanding of both simultaneously.

Rani’s Storyline: Survival in the Imperial Metropolis

The play’s invented protagonist, Rani, is a young Indian ayah who arrives at Tilbury Docks as part of a British household’s return from India. At the play’s opening, in the scene at the docks, the English family pays Rani off and leaves her without passage home. From this moment of abandonment she must navigate a London that is simultaneously the capital of the Empire she has served and a city largely hostile to her presence.

Her journey takes her into the East End, where she discovers the Lascar sailors’ community — Indian and Yemeni seafarers who have long inhabited the port districts of London — and eventually to the Ayahs’ Home, a refuge in Hackney for stranded women in her position. Gupta uses Rani’s movement through these spaces to draw a social map of the hidden Indian presence in Victorian London: domestic servants, sailors and the first tentative signs of a South Asian political community.

Key Fact

Rani’s storyline begins at Tilbury Docks when the family she worked for pays her off without a return passage. She discovers the Lascar sailors’ community in the East End and the Ayahs’ Home in Hackney — both real Victorian institutions that Gupta draws on for historical authenticity.

Abdul Karim’s Storyline: Ascent at Court

Running in parallel is the story of Abdul Karim, a historical figure who arrived at Windsor Castle in 1887 as a servant for the Golden Jubilee celebrations and rose to become Queen Victoria’s Indian secretary — her munshi. In Gupta’s dramatisation, Victoria and Abdul develop a relationship of genuine personal warmth: she learns Hindustani from him, elevates his status and protects him against the fierce hostility of the court. Lord Salisbury, the Prince of Wales and the royal household circle perceive Abdul as an inappropriate favourite and move against him repeatedly throughout the play.

The court scenes are played in sharp contrast to the East End scenes: formal, spatially rigid, visually opulent. A director might choose a proscenium arch configuration for the Windsor scenes to reinforce their theatricality and hierarchy — the court literally arranges itself for display — while the Lascar lodgings and Ayahs’ Home might be played on a thrust stage area or in a more intimate configuration to reflect communal solidarity rather than spectacle.

The Intercut Structure and Its Effect

Gupta does not tell Rani’s story to completion and then tell Abdul’s. Instead she intercuts between them scene by scene, building a pattern of parallel storylines. This structural choice carries dramaturgical weight. Every time the audience moves from a Windsor Castle scene of court conspiracy to a scene of Rani sleeping in the Ayahs’ Home, the contrast asks a question: what does the Empire mean for someone at the very top of its hierarchy, and what does it mean for someone abandoned at its edges?

The intercut structure is itself a theatrical statement. A director staging this rhythm of cuts must think carefully about transitions: how quickly do scenes change? Does music bridge the cuts? Is the set design flexible enough to shift between Windsor’s formality and the East End’s working-world warmth without a clumsy scene change? In the original RSC 2013 premiere directed by Emma Rice, ensemble multi-roling and fluid staging kept transitions fast, so that the juxtaposition landed with impact rather than interruption.

Rani is Gupta’s invented protagonist, but she is grounded in real documented history. The Ayahs’ Home in Hackney and the Lascar communities of the East End are both historically attested. Gupta has compressed and dramatised: the Ayahs’ Home opened slightly later than 1887 in reality. A strong answer recognises this as dramatic history — a playwright shaping fact for theatrical impact — rather than treating the play as a documentary record. Abdul Karim and Queen Victoria are historical; Rani and her immediate world are imaginatively reconstructed from evidence of real people in similar circumstances.

The Convergence and the Ending

The two storylines draw together near the play’s close. The moment of convergence — when Rani and figures from Abdul’s world briefly occupy the same space — offers the play’s most direct statement of solidarity. Structurally, this meeting is the fulfilment of the parallel design: two streams of late-Victorian Indian experience in Britain, briefly joined. The closing tableau asks the audience to hold in mind what has survived and what has been lost: Abdul’s papers were burned after Victoria’s death; the Ayahs’ Home closed; the Lascar community was gradually displaced.

Key Fact

The parallel, intercut structure is a deliberate dramaturgical choice: placing Rani’s world and Abdul’s world in constant dialogue means the audience cannot look at Imperial wealth without simultaneously holding in mind its human cost at street level.

When a director works on the cuts between storylines in The Empress, a useful checklist includes: (1) Lighting states — a lighting state using warm amber and gold for Windsor against a cooler, more natural white wash for the East End scenes will encode the contrast in the audience’s visual memory. (2) Underscore — Hindi or Hindustani song cues between scenes can act as bridges that carry the emotional thread of the Indian characters even into the English spaces. (3) Blocking — the physical geography of Windsor scenes (courtiers fanning out upstage in hierarchical lines) versus the East End scenes (characters gathered centre stage in an impromptu circle) communicates social structure through space alone.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For extended-response questions about structure and staging, the most common error is describing the two storylines separately rather than explaining why Gupta intercuts them and what effect that creates on an audience. Always make the juxtaposition explicit: say what the audience is made to feel or think when the Windsor scene is followed immediately by the East End scene. For a 20-mark response, answer from the performer or design perspective required by the question and address every element it names.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Empress uses a two-act structure with parallel intercut storylines: Rani’s survival story in the East End and Abdul Karim’s rise at Windsor Castle, both set in the 1887–1901 period.
  • Gupta’s structural choice to intercut rather than separate the storylines means the audience constantly holds both worlds in mind, creating dramatic irony and political contrast.
  • Directors must make active choices about how to stage transitions — through lighting state changes, underscored music and blocking patterns — to keep the intercutting fluid and the juxtaposition impactful.

practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the intercut structure (1); explanation of the technique's effect, e.g. that cutting between Rani's vulnerability and the court's opulence creates irony (1); analysis of how the structure builds towards the convergence near the play's end (1); reference to a specific named moment in one of the two storylines (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse Gupta's intentions in choosing to open The Empress with the scene at Tilbury Docks in which Rani is paid off and abandoned. What does Gupta want the audience to think and feel at this moment?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10–12): Detailed analysis of Gupta's multiple intentions — to establish Rani's vulnerability as the audience's entry point into the play; to make the systemic nature of the ayahs' exploitation concrete and immediate rather than abstract; to root the play's political argument in a personal, emotionally engaging story. Candidate links these intentions to specific dramatic methods (the choice of a public dockside setting, the power imbalance in staging terms, the contrast between Rani's isolation and the bustle of the docks) and explains the intended audience effect at each. Substantiated judgement about which intention is primary.

Upper-mid band (7–9): Two of the above intentions clearly articulated with some reference to dramatic methods; the effect on the audience is identified though not always fully developed.

Lower-mid band (4–6): One intention identified; limited reference to dramatic method; effect on audience implied rather than explained.

Low band (1–3): Describes what happens at the docks rather than analysing why Gupta chose to begin there and what she wants the audience to understand.

practice_questions.text: You are directing the moment in The Empress when the two storylines converge near the play's end and characters from Rani's world and Abdul's world briefly share the stage. How would you stage this moment to communicate the play's themes of solidarity and survival to the audience? Refer to set design, lighting, sound and at least one performer's vocal or physical choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Specific, justified choices across all four design disciplines and at least one named performer's vocal and physical choices, all anchored to this named convergence moment. Set design choice (e.g. the divide between the Windsor staging area and the East End area dissolving as characters cross the stage threshold), lighting choice (e.g. a slow cross-fade from two separate lighting states into a unified warm gold wash as the characters meet), sound choice (e.g. a Hindi underscore that swells as they converge, then holds under the final dialogue), costume contrast still legible onstage (Rani's worn sari fabric against Abdul's court livery). Performer choice: specific vocal quality and physical positioning (proxemics) for Rani in this moment. Choices are justified with reference to what the audience is meant to feel. Substantiated directorial judgement.

Upper-mid band (11–16): Most of the design areas covered with some concrete choices; at least one named performer choice; effect on audience identified for most choices.

Lower-mid band (6–10): Some relevant staging ideas but generic (e.g. 'warm lighting', 'Indian music'); little justification of how each choice creates meaning; performer choices vague.

Low band (1–5): Basic listing of staging ideas with minimal explanation; no named performer choices; descriptive rather than analytical.

lessons.title: Characters: Rani, Abdul, Hari, Lascar and Queen
lessons.content_html:
How Character Works in The Empress

Tanika Gupta builds her characters on two axes: historical ground (some are real people; some are imaginative reconstructions of documented communities) and dramatic function (each character serves a specific structural and thematic purpose). As a performer or designer approaching this play, your task is to translate character motivation into concrete, physical choices: how does Rani hold her body the moment the English family leaves the docks without her? How does Abdul Karim’s physical bearing change between his early months of nervous service and his later confidence as Victoria’s munshi?

Rani: The Invented Protagonist

Rani is the play’s moral centre. She has no historical name because the ayahs whose lives Gupta draws on largely went unrecorded, but the research behind her is real. Her character arc moves from abandonment and isolation through community — the Lascar sailors, the Ayahs’ Home — to a moment of solidarity that gives the play its emotional resolution. As a performer playing Rani, you might consider how her proxemics shift across the play: isolated at the docks, downstage centre and physically contracted; in the Ayahs’ Home, beginning to expand into shared space with other women.

In terms of vocal choices, Rani’s language moves between formal English — the register she has learned in service — and her own Bengali identity. A performer might use a careful, slightly flattened English accent when addressing English characters, shifting in pitch and pace when she speaks to Lascar Mr Das or in moments of private emotion. This code-switching is itself a character choice: it tells the audience that Rani has learned to perform a certain identity for English employers, and the release from that performance is where her true character lives.

Key Fact

Rani is an invented protagonist grounded in the real history of ayahs stranded in Victorian London. Her character journey moves from isolation to community to solidarity. A strong answer specifies her vocal register shift and physical transformation across the play.

Abdul Karim: History on Stage

Abdul Karim is a historical figure and Gupta stays close to the documented record: he arrived at Windsor in 1887, became Victoria’s Indian secretary, taught her Hindustani, was resented by the court and had his papers burned by the royal household after her death. As a dramatic character, his arc is one of extraordinary ascent and ultimate erasure. A performer playing Abdul must hold these two things simultaneously: the personal warmth and intelligence of the man, and the knowledge that his story was deliberately destroyed after Victoria died.

In the court scenes, Abdul’s physical choices should communicate his dual status: the formal upright posture and deliberate, measured movements of a man who understands he is under constant scrutiny; and underneath that, the private dignity of someone with a strong sense of his own worth. Gestus is a useful concept here. Abdul’s gestus in the court scenes might be understood as a controlled stillness — the conscious management of self-presentation under an oppressive gaze.

Queen Victoria: Warmth within the System

Gupta’s Victoria is one of the play’s most nuanced characters. She is genuinely fond of Abdul, genuinely curious about India, and uses what power she has to protect him. But she is also the Empress of India — the figurehead of the system that abandons Rani at Tilbury and burns Abdul’s papers. A director must resist letting the audience simply like Victoria. The most interesting staging of Victoria keeps both of these truths visible at once. One design approach: a golden-yellow gobo pattern suggesting the rays of empire in her scenes at court, beautiful but also inescapable — the very light that flatters her power casts shadows on those around her.

Hari Mohan Lal is a dramatic composite figure inspired by the real Dadabhai Naoroji, who was elected Liberal MP for Finsbury Central in 1892 — the first South Asian MP in British parliamentary history. Gupta draws on that real political history without making Hari identical to Naoroji. A strong answer understands this as a dramaturgical choice: Gupta uses Hari to represent the emerging South Asian political voice in Britain without the legal and narrative constraints of a purely biographical depiction. This is the same technique she uses with Rani.

Hari Mohan Lal: The Political Voice

Hari represents the nascent South Asian political presence in Westminster — the first generation of Indian-born men attempting to use the tools of British democracy to argue for Indian rights. As a dramatic character he occupies a different register from Rani or Abdul: more formal in language, more conscious of being observed and judged by a hostile political world. His scenes offer the play’s most direct engagement with political argument, as opposed to personal experience. For a costume designer, Hari’s dress is a significant choice: Western tailoring that signals his assimilation into the political world, versus any remaining South Asian detail in fabric or accessory that suggests his retained identity.

Lascar Mr Das and the East End Community

The Lascar sailor characters — Mr Das and others — represent a community that was physically present in Victorian East London for generations. They are among the most settled of the play’s Indian figures: they have lodging houses, community rituals and networks of mutual support. A designer staging the Lascar lodgings might choose a set made from found maritime objects — rope, canvas, battered sea-chests — to communicate both the nautical origin of this community and the resourcefulness of people who have built a home from whatever they could carry. Warm, low-level lighting specials could suggest lamplight and enclosure: a hidden world behind the docks.

The English Antagonists: Lord Salisbury, Bertie and Mrs Wormwood

The English antagonist figures are not cartoons of villainy. Lord Salisbury and the Prince of Wales are motivated by a genuine belief in hierarchical order: for them, Abdul’s elevation is not merely an affront to taste but a threat to the system that underpins their world. Mrs Wormwood, the English mistress who pays Rani off at the docks, may not even understand herself as doing harm. A director might use proxemics to communicate these power dynamics spatially: in the docks scene, Mrs Wormwood placed upstage, elevated on a trunk or step, with Rani standing downstage left, physically smaller in the frame, reinforces the power asymmetry before a word is spoken.

Key Fact

The English antagonists — Lord Salisbury, Bertie, Mrs Wormwood — are more effective dramatically when staged as people defending a system they believe in, rather than as simple villains. This makes the play’s argument about Empire more unsettling and more honest.

The most sophisticated performer approach to Abdul Karim holds two traditions in tension. Stanislavski’s method asks: what is Abdul’s specific inner life at each moment? What does he want from Victoria in their Hindustani lessons? What does he feel when the court conspires against him? This psychological specificity keeps him real and sympathetic. Brecht’s method asks: what is Abdul’s social gestus? What does his physical presence tell the audience about the relationship between an Indian man and an Imperial court? Both questions matter. A great performance of Abdul does not choose between them: it lets the intimate Stanislavskian truth carry the Brechtian political argument without forcing it.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark performer question, the most common error is writing about what the character feels without translating that feeling into specific vocal and physical choices. Do not write “I would play Rani as sad and frightened” — instead write: “I would play Rani with a low, controlled volume in the docks scene, a slight tightening of the jaw and a stillness of the hands that reads as suppressed panic, her gaze tracking the departing English family while her body remains rigid rather than reaching after them.” Every emotion must become a named vocal quality and a named physical action anchored to a specific moment of the play.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Rani is the play’s invented protagonist grounded in the real history of ayahs; her character arc moves from isolation to solidarity and her vocal code-switching between English and Bengali registers is a key dramatic tool.
  • Abdul Karim and Queen Victoria are historical figures; Gupta’s dramatic treatment of them holds personal warmth and Imperial complicity in tension simultaneously.
  • Staging character relationships through proxemics — placing characters in relation to each other on stage — communicates power, status and emotional truth before any dialogue is spoken.

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Rani in the moment she realises the English family has left without arranging her return passage, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to communicate her situation to the audience. Refer to specific performer skills.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7–8): Specific named vocal choice anchored to this moment (e.g. a drop in volume to barely above a whisper, a lengthened pause before she speaks her first reaction, a flattening of pitch that drains emotion from her voice as shock sets in) AND a specific named physical choice (e.g. a stillness spreading from her hands outward, a slight forward lean then arrested as she registers the absence, a controlled facial expression that suppresses panic behind a mask of dignity). Both choices are justified with reference to what this communicates to the audience about Rani's inner life and her external situation. Candidate demonstrates awareness of how these choices set up Rani's character for the rest of the play.

Upper-mid band (5–6): Clear vocal and physical choices, both relevant to this moment; some justification of the audience effect; not fully developed for both choices.

Lower-mid band (3–4): At least one valid performer choice, but described in general terms (e.g. 'I would look shocked') without specifying the exact vocal quality or physical action.

Low band (1–2): Basic description of what Rani feels with little or no translation into named vocal or physical skills.

practice_questions.text: As a director, explain how you would stage the scene in The Empress in which Abdul Karim first appears in Victoria's household to communicate both his personal dignity and his precarious position as a racial outsider at court. Refer to set design, lighting, performer choices and proxemics.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Specific, justified staging choices across all required areas. Set design: use of levels, Victorian interior materials (heavy drapes, a formal dais for Victoria's chair) that communicate court hierarchy; a clear sightline across which Abdul must cross to reach Victoria. Lighting: a warm directional spotlight on Victoria's space contrasted with the cooler, more exposed ambient light in which Abdul stands, making him visible and scrutinised. Performer (Abdul): specific physical choices communicating controlled dignity (upright posture, measured pace, deliberate stillness of the hands) and the inner cost of that control (a fractional hesitation before each courtly gesture). Proxemics: the court figures arranged upstage in a semi-circle that encloses the space Abdul must enter, so that the stage architecture itself embodies the hostile gaze. Costume: Abdul's court livery as a sign of his official role, but in a cut or colour that marks him as different from the English courtiers. All choices justified with reference to the intended effect on the audience and the play's wider themes.

Upper-mid band (11–16): Most areas covered with concrete choices; proxemics and at least two design disciplines addressed; performer choices present; effect on audience identified.

Lower-mid band (6–10): Some relevant ideas but generic descriptions; limited justification; one or more areas missing.

Low band (1–5): Basic listing of staging ideas with minimal explanation; no named performer choices; descriptive rather than analytical.

lessons.title: Themes: Empire, Race, Servitude, Solidarity
lessons.content_html:
How Theme Works in Drama

Themes in a play are not abstract ideas floating above the action: they are embodied in staging choices, costume decisions, lighting states and the physical relationships between performers. When Gupta writes about Empire in The Empress, she is writing about something that manifests in where people stand, how they speak, what fabric they wear and who holds the lantern above the scene. Your job as a performer or designer is to ask: how do I make this theme visible in the specific moment I am working on?

Theme 1: Empire as Lived Experience

The British Empire in The Empress is not a political slogan but an environment in which every character lives. For Rani, it is the system that carried her to Britain as domestic labour and left her stranded. For Abdul Karim, it is the framework within which an extraordinary personal ascent is possible — and ultimately the power that erases his legacy. For Queen Victoria, it is the vast dominion over which she feels personal pride and responsibility, without always seeing its human cost. Gupta’s dramaturgical intention is to make all three perspectives visible simultaneously, so that the audience cannot hold a single, simple view of what the Empire was.

A designer staging the Empire theme might consider: in the Windsor scenes, a lighting wash in deep gold and warm amber, with heavy draped set pieces suggesting the material weight of Imperial wealth. In contrast, the docks and the East End scenes lit with a cooler, harsher white or a pale blue-grey — the light of labour, of weather, of London’s working waterfront. The contrast is not just aesthetic: it makes the inequality legible at a glance.

Key Fact

The Empire theme in The Empress is made concrete through contrasting staging: Windsor’s opulence against the East End’s austerity. A strong design answer specifies the exact lighting state, colour, fabric or set element and explains what it communicates about power.

Theme 2: Race and Racial Hierarchy

Late Victorian Britain had its own articulated racial hierarchy, in which the British ruling class considered themselves at the apex. This theme enters the play most forcefully through the court’s reaction to Abdul Karim: their hostility to him is not merely snobbery but a specific racial refusal to accept an Indian man as a close intimate of the queen. For a performer playing Lord Salisbury or Bertie, the challenge is to embody this worldview without caricature — to show how a system of racial superiority felt, from the inside, like natural order.

Sightlines and focus are useful tools here. A director might block the court conspiracy scenes so that the English characters are placed in a closed circle from which Abdul is spatially excluded: the staging itself enacts the racial hierarchy without needing dialogue to explain it. When Abdul is then admitted to Victoria’s private space, the open blocking — the two characters facing each other across a more intimate distance — represents a rupture in the spatial logic of the court.

Theme 3: Domestic Servitude and the Hidden Labour Force

The ayahs and Lascar sailors of the play represent what historians sometimes call the Empire’s ‘shadow economy’: the Indian domestic and maritime labour that made the British way of life possible but was rendered largely invisible in the official record. Gupta makes them visible. As a designer, the Ayahs’ Home scenes offer an opportunity to stage this community with care and specificity: the domestic objects that fill the space (worn saris, cooking vessels, children’s toys brought from India) become props as symbols. A cracked teacup might have been carried from Calcutta to London; it is simultaneously an ordinary object and an emblem of displacement.

Gupta’s approach is more theatrically interesting than simple editorialising. She presents characters on all sides of the Imperial divide with specificity and interior life. Victoria is genuinely warm; Salisbury genuinely believes in order; Rani genuinely survives. The play’s argument about Empire emerges from the juxtaposition of these experiences, not from any character becoming a mouthpiece. A strong answer analyses Gupta’s dramatic method rather than simply labelling the play’s politics.

Theme 4: Language, Identity and Power

Language in The Empress is not neutral. The play features bilingual exchanges in English, Bengali and Hindustani, and the choice of which language a character speaks in any given scene is a political act. When Victoria asks Abdul to teach her Hindustani, she is crossing a cultural threshold that her court considers improper — the Queen of England learning the language of a colony. When Rani speaks Bengali in the Ayahs’ Home, she is reclaiming a private self that she suppressed in English domestic service.

For a sound designer, the bilingual texture of the play opens possibilities. Hindustani songs might be underscored beneath Abdul’s scenes with Victoria, creating a soundscape that insists the Indian world is present even in Windsor. The decision of when to hear the underscore and when to remove it can track the power dynamics of each scene: is India welcome in this space, or suppressed?

Theme 5: Solidarity and Community in the Diaspora

Against the play’s theme of Imperial exploitation, Gupta places an equally important counter-theme: solidarity. The Lascar sailors who take Rani in, the ayah community of Hackney, the early Indian political networks around Hari — these are not passive victims. They are people building community, mutual support and a shared identity in a country that official culture treats as foreign. This theme reaches its theatrical culmination in the moment of convergence near the play’s end, when Rani’s storyline and the world of Abdul and Hari briefly meet.

Key Fact

Gupta places the theme of solidarity at the same dramatic weight as the theme of Imperial exploitation. The Ayahs’ Home and Lascar community scenes must be staged with warmth and specificity — not as scenes of suffering, but as scenes of survival and community-building.

As a performer in the Ayahs’ Home scenes: Rani’s physical transformation from the contracted, isolated posture of the docks scene to an open, relaxed body in shared space is one of the play’s most important character moments. You might mark this with a deliberate unclenching of the hands, a deepening of the breath, a willingness to make eye contact across the room. Vocally, the shift from the guarded English register she uses with Mrs Wormwood to the Bengali and Hindi of the home community could be marked with a change in pitch, a faster pace and a genuine rise in volume: the sound of someone speaking in their own voice for the first time in the play.

As a designer for the same scenes: a low, warm Fresnel wash in amber-gold (echoing, at lower intensity, the Windsor palette) could suggest warmth and belonging without irony — this is not the Empire’s gold but domestic lamplight. The set might be arranged with performers in a circle at centre stage, using the in-the-round configuration (or a modified thrust) to make the audience feel included in the community rather than observing it from outside.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 12-mark question about playwright’s intentions, the most common error is describing what happens in the scene rather than analysing what Gupta wants the audience to think or feel at that moment. Every point must be double-linked: first to the dramatic method Gupta uses (e.g. a bilingual exchange, a staging contrast, a specific character gesture), then to the intended effect on the audience (e.g. “this makes the audience feel the personal cost of code-switching rather than understanding it as an abstract political argument”). For a 20-mark staging question, answer from the performer or design perspective required by the question, and justify each choice through a specific theme and a named moment.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The major themes of The Empress — Empire, race, servitude and solidarity — are not abstract; they are made concrete through specific staging choices, lighting states, costume decisions and the physical relationships between performers.
  • Language choice (English, Bengali, Hindustani) is a political act in this play; a sound designer can use language-specific underscoring to track whose world is welcome in each scene.
  • Gupta balances the theme of exploitation with the counter-theme of solidarity: the Ayahs’ Home and Lascar community scenes should be staged with warmth and community, not as scenes of suffering only.

lessons.title: Context: Victorian Britain and the Indian Diaspora
lessons.content_html:
Why Context Matters for Drama Students

Understanding the social, cultural and historical context of a set play is not a separate academic exercise — it directly informs every staging and performance choice. When you know that the Lascar sailors had been settled in East London for generations by 1887, you can make a costume choice that reflects established community rather than recent arrival. When you know that Abdul Karim’s relationship with Victoria was a matter of documented record and court controversy, you can play the hostility of the English court as something felt, not invented. Context is the raw material from which staging decisions are made concrete and justified.

1887: The Golden Jubilee Year

The play opens in 1887, the year of Queen Victoria’s Golden Jubilee — the fiftieth anniversary of her accession. The Jubilee was a carefully managed spectacle of Imperial prestige: visiting dignitaries from across the Empire, public celebrations in London, military pageants. It was also the moment when Abdul Karim first arrived at Windsor as a young Indian man recruited to serve at the festivities. Gupta uses the Jubilee as a dramatic counterpoint: the public display of Imperial unity set against the private abandonment of women like Rani on the docks below.

For a designer, the Jubilee context opens specific aesthetic possibilities. Victorian royal ceremony had a known visual vocabulary: deep crimson and gold, military uniforms, gauze backdrops suggesting ceremonial grandeur. A director might use this vocabulary deliberately for the Windsor scenes and then undercut it: the same crimson and gold light that glamorises the Jubilee procession might, in a different scene, feel oppressive rather than celebratory when it falls on Abdul rather than on the English court.

Key Fact

1887 was the year of Victoria’s Golden Jubilee and the year Abdul Karim arrived at Windsor. Gupta uses the Jubilee as an ironic framing: the public spectacle of Empire at its height, set against the private abandonment of Rani at Tilbury Docks on the same day.

The British Raj and the Empress of India

Britain had ruled India directly since 1858, after the East India Company’s authority was dissolved following the uprising of 1857. Queen Victoria was formally declared Empress of India in 1876 — a title added at the suggestion of Benjamin Disraeli to make explicit the Imperial relationship. By 1887, India was the jewel of the Empire in official rhetoric: the source of enormous economic value, the proving ground for the British civil service, the largest territory under the Crown.

The practical human consequence of this relationship was a constant flow of Indian people into Britain: domestic servants accompanying colonial families on home leave, sailors recruited for British merchant shipping, traders and students, and eventually political figures such as Dadabhai Naoroji. The Empress stages the human texture of this flow — the real people whose arrival and often stranding in London the official Jubilee narrative had no place for.

The Ayahs and Their Home

The Ayahs’ Home in Hackney was a real institution: a hostel established by Christian missionaries to provide accommodation for Indian women stranded in London when the families they had travelled with could not or would not pay for their return. Gupta has placed the opening of the Ayahs’ Home slightly earlier than its actual documented date for dramatic compression. This is a standard technique in dramatic history: the playwright is not writing a documentary but using real institutions to give her invented characters authentic ground to stand on.

For a set designer, the Ayahs’ Home offers a richly specific environment: a Victorian terrace interior in Hackney, furnished with both English middle-class missionary taste (plain wooden furniture, Christian images) and the Indian domestic objects the women brought with them. The collision of these two aesthetics in the set dressing communicates the cultural in-between world the women inhabit — not fully at home in India because they are in England, not fully belonging to England because they are Indian.

The slight compression of the Ayahs’ Home timeline is a deliberate dramaturgical choice, not a historical error. Show this understanding: Gupta is writing dramatic history, which means she shapes and compresses real events to serve the play’s dramatic and thematic needs. The play is not a history textbook and should not be judged as one. What matters is that the Ayahs’ Home was real, ayahs were really stranded in London, and the community that helped them was real — Gupta has brought these true facts onto the stage at the most dramatically compelling moment.

Lascar Sailors and the East London Community

The term “Lascar” referred broadly to Indian and South Asian sailors employed on British merchant ships. By the Victorian era, long-established Lascar communities existed in the dock districts of East London, particularly around Shadwell and the East India Dock. These communities had their own lodging houses, community networks and cultural practices. They were part of the city’s life, yet largely invisible to the official Victorian narrative of London.

As a designer staging the Lascar lodgings, the combination of maritime objects and South Asian domestic culture is the key to the scene’s atmosphere. Set design elements such as coiled rope, sea-chests, canvas and lanterns sit alongside cooking smells suggested by warm amber footlights and the sound of a Bengali folksong — a diegetic soundscape emanating from within the scene rather than externally applied.

Abdul Karim: The Historical Record

The historical Abdul Karim (c. 1863–1909) arrived at Windsor in June 1887. His relationship with Victoria is documented in her own diaries and in the diaries and letters of hostile courtiers. Victoria promoted him from personal attendant to Indian clerk to munshi; she asked to be taught Hindustani; she gave him a house and brought him to Scotland and the south of France on her travels. After her death in 1901, her son and heir Edward VII immediately had Abdul’s papers, diaries and letters burned and expelled him from Britain. The deliberate erasure of his record was itself a statement about whose history was permitted to exist.

Gupta stages this erasure as the play’s closing movement. For a lighting designer, the moment when Abdul’s world at court is systematically dismantled might use a slow fade to black for specific parts of the Windsor set while the rest of the stage remains lit — the physical erasure of his space mirroring the historical destruction of his papers.

Tanika Gupta and the RSC Commission

Tanika Gupta MBE was born in London in 1965 to parents of Bengali heritage. She has written extensively for the stage and television, and her work consistently returns to the experience of South Asian people within British history. The Empress was commissioned by the Royal Shakespeare Company for the Swan Theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, and premiered there in 2013 under the direction of Emma Rice. An RSC commission is a significant artistic statement: the institution most associated with Shakespeare’s canonical English cultural heritage choosing to stage a play that recovers the Indian presence within the British story. The RSC revival in 2023 at the Lyric Hammersmith, directed by Pooja Ghai, brought the play back into public view with a second major production.

Key Fact

The Empress was commissioned by the RSC and premiered at the Swan Theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, in 2013, directed by Emma Rice. The RSC’s commissioning choice was itself culturally significant: Gupta’s play brings the Indian presence in British history into the home of canonical British theatre.

Gupta is part of a tradition of Black and Asian British theatre-makers who have used the stage to recover histories excluded from mainstream cultural narrative. Her work shares ground with playwrights such as Winsome Pinnock, Roy Williams and Kwame Kwei-Armah, and with companies including the Tara Theatre and Tamasha, which have developed South Asian British theatre over several decades. Understanding this context helps students see The Empress not only as a history play but as an intervention in the question of whose history gets told on Britain’s major stages. The RSC commission brought that question to the most establishment of venues, with considerable dramaturgical intent.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions that ask about context, examiners do not want a list of historical facts — they want to see you applying context to specific staging decisions. Every contextual detail you raise should be followed immediately by its design or performance implication: “Because the Lascar community had been in East London for generations by 1887, a set designer might choose worn but carefully maintained domestic objects that signal established community rather than recent arrival — communicating permanence and belonging, which contrasts with Rani’s displacement.” For a 12-mark intentions question framed around context, show Gupta’s specific dramaturgical choice: why did she write this play for the RSC in 2013? What did she want a contemporary audience to understand about British history that the official narrative omits?
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The play is set in 1887, the year of Victoria’s Golden Jubilee, and draws on real institutions (the Ayahs’ Home, the Lascar community) and real people (Abdul Karim, loosely Dadabhai Naoroji) while using dramatic compression to serve the play’s theatrical needs.
  • Abdul Karim’s papers were burned after Victoria’s death — a historical erasure that Gupta stages as part of the play’s closing movement, using the production’s design vocabulary to make the destruction visible.
  • Gupta was commissioned by the RSC for the 2013 premiere; understanding the significance of that commissioning context helps students analyse her dramaturgical intentions for a contemporary audience.

practice_questions.text: You are designing the production of The Empress for a large proscenium arch theatre. How would you use set design, lighting, sound and costume to communicate the contrast between the Golden Jubilee world of Windsor and the hidden world of the Lascar community and the Ayahs' Home to the audience? Refer to specific design choices for both worlds.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Specific, justified choices across all four design disciplines applied to both worlds, with clear contrast between them. Windsor set design: raised levels, heavy drape or gauze backcloth in crimson and gold, a formal chair or dais for Victoria, sightlines that place the court in a hierarchy legible from every seat. Lascar/Ayahs' Home set design: lower, warmer space at stage level, maritime and domestic objects as props-as-symbols, no raised platform. Windsor lighting: deep gold and amber wash with a profile lantern special on Victoria's seat; profile lanterns for the court to create a sense of official illumination. East End lighting: warm low-level Fresnel wash, no specials, the suggestion of lamplight rather than stage light. Windsor sound: minimal, perhaps a formal orchestral underscore hinting at Victorian ceremony. East End sound: a diegetic soundscape with Bengali or Hindustani song from within the scene. Windsor costume: deep crimson and gilt for Victoria, black formal English tailoring for the court, Abdul's court livery marking him as different. lessons.title: Dramatic Methods: Languages, Letters and Songs
lessons.content_html:
Language as Power on Stage

One of Tanika Gupta’s most distinctive dramatic methods in The Empress is her use of code-switching — moving between English, Bengali and Hindustani in the same conversation. This is not decorative. Every time a character shifts language, Gupta signals something precise: who holds power, who is excluded, and what a character guards as their own. When Rani and Mr Das speak Bengali to each other in the Lascar lodging-house scenes, the English characters in the room are shut out. The audience experiences, briefly, the same exclusion that Indian people experienced daily in Victorian Britain.

For a performer, delivering a bilingual scene demands close attention to accent and register. When Rani speaks to Mrs Wormwood, her English becomes careful, softened, deferential — lower pitch, measured pace, pauses before answering, a posture slightly inclined forward. The same actress playing the Lascar lodging-house scene can stand straighter, speak faster, a wider pitch range; her body reads the difference in status without the audience needing it explained.

Key Fact

The bilingual exchanges in The Empress work politically as well as theatrically: they remind the audience that English is the colonisers’ language, and that speaking it demands a performance of compliance from Indian characters. This is language as subtext — what is not said in English is as significant as what is.

Letters: Private Voices in Public History

Gupta uses epistolary staging throughout the play. Abdul Karim writes letters home to India; Rani struggles to find someone who will carry her words back across the ocean. A director staging these letter sequences faces a choice about staging configuration. In a theatre in the round configuration, a character reading a letter aloud becomes a private act watched by all — intimate and surrounded. In a proscenium arch configuration, a single spotlight isolating the letter-writer against a dark stage creates formality and distance, underlining the historical gulf between writer and reader.

The design possibilities for letter scenes are rich. A lighting designer might use a lighting special — a narrow profile spot — to hold the letter-writer in a pool of warm amber, suggesting both candlelight and memory. Sound could underpin these moments with a sparse Indian underscore: perhaps a single sitar phrase, unresolved, fading as the letter ends. The costume worn in letter scenes can be a design signal too: if Abdul writes home wearing both his Indian robes and a British-issued badge of office, the visual contradiction speaks volumes without a word.

Students sometimes argue that bilingual dialogue is simply there for historical authenticity — “they would have spoken Bengali in real life.” This loses marks. Gupta makes deliberate theatrical choices about when characters switch language and who is present. The dramatic question is always: what does the language shift do to the audience at this moment? Treat code-switching as a staging device with the same intentionality as a lighting change or a costume reveal.

Hindi Songs: the Brechtian Interrupt

Gupta includes Hindi songs and Indian music as a structural device. When the song interrupts the naturalistic action, the fourth wall becomes porous. This is a Brechtian effect: the emotional flow is paused; the audience is reminded it is watching a constructed history, not simply watching life. A sound designer staging the songs must decide whether the music comes from onstage musicians (diegetic — the characters can hear it too), from offstage (non-diegetic — felt but not seen), or from a recorded soundscape that places the song in the characters’ memory rather than their present.

A performer who delivers a Hindi song must choose whether to break eye contact with the other characters and address the audience directly. This is direct address: the character becomes a narrator of their own story. The physical choices here matter — does the performer stand still, commanding the stage? Or do they move through the space, making eye contact with audience members in different seats? Either choice communicates something about whether Rani (or Abdul) feels seen by the world watching them.

Key Fact

The songs in The Empress are not musical-theatre entertainment — they are political interruptions. Like the songs in Brecht’s epic theatre, they comment on the action rather than advancing it. They ask the audience to reflect on what they have just seen.

Direct Address and Victorian Registers

Gupta also contrasts the heightened formality of Victorian English court dialogue with the less formal registers of the Lascar lodging house and Rani’s scenes. When British court characters speak, their language is measured, ceremonially polite and opaque — meaning hidden behind etiquette. A performer playing Lord Salisbury or a courtier might adopt a clipped vocal quality: precise consonants, restrained volume, almost no pitch variation. The stillness is threatening. Contrast this with Rani’s scenes, where the dialogue can be direct, warmly colloquial, even comic — serving both character and political point. The audience roots for the more expressive voice.

Direct address is used particularly for Rani. When she steps forward and speaks to the audience, the staging must support this. A lighting designer might shift from the general lighting wash to a front-facing special, pulling her out of the scene. The sound designer might remove the ambient underscore entirely — silence framing her words. These design choices signal: this moment is outside the fiction; hear it differently.

As a performer: In the moment Rani first turns to address the audience from the Tilbury Docks scene, you might step forward from the tableau of the dock, pause for two full beats, make deliberate eye contact with a section of the audience — not a single person, but a sweep — then speak at a moderate pace with a slight raising of pitch on the key phrase, signalling that she is asking a question of the world, not just narrating. Your posture is upright but not rigid: dignity without defiance yet. Arms loose at your sides, hands slightly open. Proxemics matter: you place yourself downstage centre, separating yourself from the English family grouping behind you upstage.

As a designer: As the lighting designer you fade the general wash to 20% and bring up a single 650w profile spot from a front-of-house position, colour temperature a warm 2800K amber (suggesting both gaslight and a remembered warmth), no gobo. As the sound designer you drop the ambient dock soundscape (gulls, rigging, crowd murmur) to silence on her first step forward, replacing it with nothing — the silence itself becomes a sound cue that isolates her in time.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 12-mark question on playwright’s intentions, students commonly describe events — “Rani speaks Bengali to show she is Indian” — instead of analysing what Gupta wants the audience to think, feel or understand at that moment. The command word “analyse” demands you identify the intention, then explain how the dramatic method achieves it, then judge the effect on the audience. For a bilingual scene, a Mastering answer might argue: Gupta uses code-switching here to make the audience feel the discomfort of linguistic exclusion, placing them in solidarity with Rani rather than with the English family — a political alignment disguised as naturalistic detail. For extended-response questions, always anchor your analysis of language to a specific named moment of the play and show how a performer or designer could heighten that effect.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Code-switching between English, Bengali and Hindustani is a political device, not decoration — it signals power, exclusion and identity, and demands specific vocal and physical choices from performers.
  • Letters and direct address allow Gupta to give private voices a public stage — lighting specials, silence and a shift in proxemics can all signal these moments of testimony to the audience.
  • Hindi songs function as Brechtian interruptions: they pause the emotional flow and ask the audience to witness and reflect rather than simply feel.

lessons.title: Staging and Design: Docks, Drawing Rooms and Court
lessons.content_html:
The Design Challenge: Three Worlds, One Stage

The Empress moves constantly between three distinct worlds — Tilbury Docks and the East End streets, the Ayahs’ Home in Hackney, and the interior of Windsor Castle. Each world carries its own class, race and power dynamic, and the designer’s task is to communicate this visually without lengthy explanatory dialogue. The fundamental design choice is about set design: does the production use a fully realistic set for each world, or a shared, flexible stylised staging concept?

Most productions of Gupta’s play favour a fluid, semi-abstract approach: a permanent architectural framework on stage that can read as a dockside, a domestic interior, or a royal chamber depending on how it is lit and populated with props. This approach allows rapid scene transitions between Rani’s world and Abdul’s without blackouts and lengthy set changes breaking the play’s momentum. The designer might use raised platforms at different levels: upstage elevated areas for Windsor Castle interiors, lower ground-level areas for the dockside — staging status literally into the geography of the stage.

Key Fact

A designer’s choices in The Empress must work politically as well as practically. The contrast between the East End’s raw materials (rope, crates, damp stone, gas lamps) and Windsor’s opulence (gilded surfaces, velvet, chandeliers) is not just period detail — it is a visual argument about imperial inequality.

Set Design: Dock, Home and Court

For the Tilbury Docks opening, a set designer might use a bare stage with a few heavy wooden crates and lengths of rope coiled on the floor. The texture is rough — raw timber, perhaps a patch of water-stained canvas. Props as symbols are powerful here: the single bag that contains everything Rani owns signals her precariousness as soon as it is placed in the performance space. Sightlines matter. In an end-on configuration, the dock could fill the full width of the stage, placing the audience in the position of spectators on the quay watching the ship arrive. In a traverse configuration, the dock becomes a corridor — the characters move through it, and the audience on both sides feel enclosed by it.

For Windsor Castle, the design language shifts completely. A gilded frame or a pair of high-backed chairs might be sufficient to signal the court. Period-detail wallpaper projected via a lighting gobo onto a plain cyclorama can transform a bare wall into an ornate Victorian interior without building a full set — and it can be removed instantly by a simple lighting cross-fade, returning the stage to neutral for the next scene in the East End.

Lighting Design: Dividing the World

Lighting is the key design tool for managing the play’s parallel storylines. A director using split staging can hold both Rani’s East End scene and Abdul’s court scene live on stage at the same time, cross-fading between them. The choice of colour temperature communicates world without words: a cool, blue-grey lighting state for the docks (suggesting overcast London skies and industrial cold), a warm amber-gold wash for Windsor (suggesting wealth, firelight, warmth used ironically given the coldness of the court politics within).

Specific lantern choices matter in an exam answer. A Fresnel flood with a half-CTO (colour temperature orange) gel gives the warm diffuse quality appropriate for the Ayahs’ Home — soft-edged, domestic, communal. A profile spot with a harder edge and a steel-blue gel, angled steeply from above, can make the dock scene feel exposed and cold. A moving light programmed to track Rani through the dock space underlines her isolation: she moves, the light follows, the rest of the stage stays dark.

Many students write “I would use period lighting to create a Victorian atmosphere.” This scores Developing at best. Period lighting is not a design choice — it is a vague intention. You need to specify: what type of lantern? What gel or colour temperature? What direction? What intensity? What effect does this specific combination produce, and why does it serve this moment’s meaning? A Mastering answer names the lantern (profile, Fresnel, flood), the colour (amber, steel blue, straw), the direction (front-of-house, overhead, side), and links it explicitly to the scene’s power dynamics.

Sound Design: From Dockside to Palace

The sound cue is one of the fastest design tools for switching world. A sound designer for The Empress might build a dockside soundscape from: the low rumble of steam engines, the creak of wooden hulls, water lapping against stone, and the cries of dock workers mixing in English and Lascar languages. This can be cross-faded on a single cue into the measured formality of a string quartet minuet for the Windsor scenes — a sound transition that in itself makes an argument about the gulf between these worlds.

Indian music as underscore in Rani’s scenes and the Lascar lodging house signals cultural belonging and memory. A sound designer might use a sitar phrase or a tabla pattern, low in the mix during dialogue (non-diegetic), swelling briefly during moments of solidarity or joy, then cutting out entirely for the scenes where Rani is most isolated. The sudden silence in the middle of the dockside scene — no underscore, no ambient sound — can be more powerful than any sound cue.

Costume Design: Fabric as Political Argument

Costume in The Empress is one of the richest areas for design discussion. The visual contrast between Indian and British dress is immediately legible to the audience, but a sophisticated designer moves beyond “Indian costume versus Victorian costume”. Rani as an ayah might wear a cotton sari in a muted, washed-out colour — suggesting both Indian heritage and the fading that comes from service and poverty. The fabric drapes naturally but is worn and practical. If she is given a British-style apron or service uniform over the sari, the layering communicates her in-between status: Indian body, British domestic service.

Abdul Karim’s costume charts his change in status. Arriving in British-issued servant’s uniform, he might later be seen in embroidered Indian court dress bestowed by Victoria — but the embroidery is read differently by different characters on stage. To Victoria it is honour; to Lord Salisbury it is presumption. The designer can make this argument visible: perhaps the court figures literally look away from Abdul’s robes while Victoria leans forward. Proxemics and blocking reinforces the costume’s argument without adding a word of dialogue.

Multi-roling is a structural feature of The Empress: the British court figures and minor English characters are often doubled or trebled among the ensemble cast. A costume designer must make multi-roling legible to the audience through a clear, quick system of transformation — a tailcoat on or off, a hat changed, a wig removed. The challenge is that each transformation must read instantly from the auditorium. One approach: design the British court figures’ costumes as a single visual “kit” (black tail coat, white cravat, top hat) that can be assembled and disassembled in seconds behind a set piece, while the Indian characters’ costumes are more individual and varied — a visual argument that the British establishment are interchangeable functionaries where the Indian characters are distinct people.

Multi-roling through costume transformation

British court characters in The Empress can be designed as a matching kit — tailcoat, cravat, top hat — assembled and removed in seconds, making the establishment interchangeable while Indian characters remain visually distinct individuals.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a design question, the most common error is giving one idea per discipline without justifying it: “I would use warm lighting for Windsor” earns one mark. The examiner needs the specific choice (Fresnel, amber gel, direction: overhead), the effect on the audience (warmth is ironic given the court’s hostility to Abdul), and the named moment it applies to (the scene where Abdul first serves Victoria). That is three levels of thought from one lantern. Aim to develop every design choice to that third level. For the 20-mark extended response, answer from the performer or design perspective required by the question, anchored to a named scene or moment. A common error is drifting from the named focus and writing a general production design answer — stay on the specific scene throughout.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Set, lighting and sound must work together to signal the three worlds of The Empress (docks, East End, Windsor) with speed and political clarity — named lanterns, fabrics, gels and sound textures score far higher than vague period references.
  • Costume is a political argument: the contrast between Indian dress and British imperial uniform communicates the play’s power dynamics without a word of dialogue, especially when combined with proxemics and blocking.
  • Multi-roling of British court figures is a design-in-performance challenge — costumes must be quick-change systems that read instantly from the auditorium while making the argument that the establishment figures are interchangeable.

lessons.title: Performance Interpretation: Rani Standing Her Ground
lessons.content_html:
What Performance Interpretation Means in This Play

Every character in The Empress navigates the same central tension: how to maintain dignity while navigating the structures of British imperial power. As a performer, your task is not to choose whether your character is “angry” or “sad” — it is to find the precise vocal quality and physical shape that communicates what a specific character guards under pressure. Vocal interpretation and physical interpretation are the two instruments available. In Drama, naming the emotion is not enough — you must translate the emotion into a concrete, observable choice.

The four key characters for performance analysis are: Rani, whose journey is from abandoned vulnerability to quiet defiance; Abdul Karim, whose arc moves from nervous deference to grounded confidence; Hari Mohan Lal, who carries the political voice of educated Indian ambition; and Queen Victoria, whose private warmth exists in ironic tension with the Empire she represents.

Rani: Quiet Defiance

The most important performance principle for Rani is that her resistance is almost never loud. When Mrs Wormwood pays her off at Tilbury Docks, a performer who plays Rani’s response as overt anger will lose the scene’s power. The more interesting choice is stillness: Rani holds her ground physically — feet planted, proxemics held at exactly the distance of a servant who refuses to back away — while her vocal volume drops rather than rises. A lower, measured voice, slower pace, distinct pauses before each reply. The pauses are doing the work: they say “I am choosing not to perform the gratitude you expect.”

In the Ayahs’ Home scenes and the Lascar lodging-house scenes, the same performer can open the physical and vocal register completely. Here Rani’s posture is relaxed, her gestures broader, her pitch warmer and more variable. The contrast between these registers tells the audience the full story of what the docks scene cost her. A director might stage these community scenes with Rani downstage, drawing the audience into her community, while the English characters always occupy the upstage area — a spatial argument about whose world this is.

Key Fact

A common error in performance questions is describing what the character feels rather than what the performer does. “Rani feels hurt and betrayed” is interior analysis. “The performer drops vocal volume, slows pace, holds eye contact with Mrs Wormwood for three full beats before turning away with a controlled exhale” is performance interpretation. Write the second kind of answer.

Abdul Karim: Growing Confidence

Abdul arrives at Windsor Castle as a servant who speaks English and is acutely aware of his visible difference. The performer’s opening physical choices should communicate this: shoulders slightly forward, head inclined, movements precise and measured — the body of someone who does not want to take up too much space. A performer could begin with English that is over-articulated, effortful and pitched upward slightly as though each sentence is a question. As his relationship with Victoria develops, these choices can shift: he stands taller, occupies the centre of the stage space more readily, his voice finding a lower, steadier register.

The moment the court conspires against Abdul is a key performance opportunity. The performer playing Abdul in those scenes might use tableau-quality stillness — standing entirely motionless while the English characters move and scheme around him — as a way of communicating his dignity under threat. The stillness is more powerful than movement here: the audience reads it as refusal to perform the panic the court wants to provoke. A lighting designer can heighten this by keeping Abdul in a steady warm lighting state while the scheming courtiers are cast in cooler, more fragmented light.

Consider the scene when Abdul first teaches Victoria a Hindustani word. A Stanislavskian approach asks both performers to find the specific, small truth of the moment: Victoria’s genuine delight and Abdul’s carefully restrained pleasure at being valued rather than dismissed. The performer playing Victoria might lean forward slightly, her posture losing its regal formality for just a moment — a physical signal of private warmth. The performer playing Abdul might allow a brief, controlled smile: eyes warm, a slight release of the permanent slight tension in his shoulders, but the smile does not break into a full grin, because he has learned not to display joy openly in this house. These small, specific choices communicate the relationship’s complexity to the audience more effectively than a larger emotional display.

Queen Victoria: Public and Private

Victoria is one of the most demanding performance challenges in the play because a strong answer holds two contradictory truths about her simultaneously: her genuine warmth towards Abdul is real, and her role as the symbolic head of an Empire that brutalises Rani’s community is equally real. A performer who plays her as a simple imperial villain misses the play’s argument; a performer who plays her as a warm grandmother ignores the structural critique. The key is to show the difference between her public and private registers.

In public court scenes, the performer might use a formal physical posture — upright, hands folded, gaze fixed, deliberate formal diction with full consonants — the performance of imperial authority. In private scenes with Abdul, the same performer can soften: a slight forward lean, a lower vocal register (warmer, less projected), eye contact that admits rather than commands. The transition between these registers, managed precisely and consistently, communicates the play’s central argument about how power works: Victoria can be kind and still be the Empress of India.

Hari Mohan Lal: The Political Voice

Hari carries the explicitly political argument of the play: that Indian people belong in British public life not as servants or curiosities but as citizens and legislators. The performer playing Hari must navigate a different version of the code-switching challenge: Hari speaks entirely in formal Victorian English register, and the risk is that this makes him sound like a British establishment figure rather than an Indian one. The choice might be to maintain a clearly Indian accent throughout, refusing to assimilate vocally even when the words are entirely correct. His physicality might be erect and formal — the body of someone who has studied the gestus of parliamentary authority — but with a stillness and groundedness that is distinctly different from the restless energy of the English political figures around him.

Key Fact

For performance questions in the exam, always anchor your choices to a specific named moment. “Throughout the play” is too vague to score Mastering. “In the moment Abdul is confronted by Lord Salisbury after Victoria’s first lesson, I would drop vocal volume to near-inaudible and stand completely still at centre stage” is the level of specificity to aim for.

Students sometimes try to resolve Victoria’s complexity by choosing a single reading: either she is a kind old woman and the Empire is just context, or she is a hypocrite whose warmth to Abdul is meaningless given the system she heads. Gupta’s writing holds both truths in tension and a strong answer maintains that tension in their performance analysis. The challenge is not to resolve the contradiction but to perform it: Victoria’s genuine warmth is what makes the structural critique more devastating, not less. A performer who can show both is doing justice to the play’s argument.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark performer question, the most common error is describing emotion without translating it into observable choices. Writing “Rani would feel angry and upset” earns no marks. The question asks how you as a performer would communicate that state through vocal and physical choices anchored to a named moment. Structure your answer: name the moment, state the vocal choice (pitch, pace, volume, pause, accent), state the physical choice (posture, gesture, proxemics, use of space), then justify each choice by explaining its effect on the audience. A Mastering answer will include at least one vocal and one physical choice, both specific enough that a director could use the description in a rehearsal note, both anchored to the same named moment, and both linked to what they communicate to the audience about the character’s situation.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Rani’s defiance is communicated through stillness and a controlled vocal register, not through raised volume — the specific physical and vocal choices communicate far more than a general emotional label.
  • Abdul’s arc from anxious deference to grounded confidence must be tracked through changing posture, proxemics and vocal register across the play — not stated but physically performed.
  • Victoria’s performance complexity lies in holding her genuine warmth to Abdul alongside her structural role as Empress of India — the contradiction should be performed, not resolved.

lessons.title: Practitioner Application: Brecht and Documentary History
lessons.content_html:
Why Practitioners Matter in This Play

When applying a practitioner’s ideas to a set play, do not give a biography of Brecht or Stanislavski. Instead ask: how do specific techniques from a practitioner’s practice shape the way the play is performed and designed? In The Empress, Gupta draws on two distinct theatrical traditions that pull in different directions — and understanding why she uses both is the key to a sophisticated answer.

Bertolt Brecht developed what he called epic theatre, a mode in which the audience is reminded that they are watching a constructed event, not reality. The purpose was political: Brecht wanted audiences to reflect on social systems and imagine alternatives, rather than losing themselves in emotional identification with characters. His techniques include direct address, songs that interrupt the action, narrative captions, ensemble multi-roling, and gestus — physical actions that reveal social roles rather than psychological interiority.

Key Fact

Gupta’s stated aim in writing The Empress was to bring hidden histories to the stage — to make visible the Indian people who lived in Victorian Britain but whose presence was written out of the official record. This is a Brechtian project: the audience’s role is to witness and recognise, not just to watch and feel.

Brechtian Techniques in The Empress

The play’s use of direct address is openly Brechtian. When Rani steps forward and speaks to the audience, she is functioning as a narrator of her own story as much as a character within it. Brecht called this the alienation effect (or Verfremdungseffekt): the audience is pulled out of emotional absorption and asked to process what they are seeing as a witness rather than as a participant. A director staging these moments of direct address can reinforce the Brechtian signal through design: lights shift to a cool, even lighting wash rather than an intimate special, breaking the illusion of the scene’s naturalistic world.

The Hindi songs serve a similar function. Brecht used songs in his plays not to advance the plot emotionally but to comment on the action and interrupt the audience’s feeling with a moment of reflection. When a Hindi song rises in The Empress, the naturalistic drama pauses. The audience is given space to think about what the song’s presence means: this is not just Rani’s private world — it is a culture, a community, a history that predates the Empire and refuses to be absorbed by it. A sound designer staging the songs as fully amplified, theatrically lit events (perhaps with a sudden change in the lighting state, a bright full-stage wash without shadow) underlines the Brechtian rupture.

Brecht’s concept of gestus is particularly useful for the British court figures in The Empress. A director using a Brechtian approach might instruct the performers playing Lord Salisbury, Bertie and the household to adopt a set of repeated, recognisable gestures that expose their social role rather than creating rounded psychological characters: a slight backward lean when confronted with anything un-English, hands clasped behind the back in a posture of proprietary authority, a collective turning of backs towards Abdul. These gestural choices would be deliberately stylised rather than naturalistic — almost choreographic in their coordination — so that the audience sees the court as a social institution rather than a collection of individuals. The multi-roling of these figures reinforces this: if one performer plays three different court functionaries, the gestus must be consistent across all three, making the point that the faces change but the power structure does not.

Stanislavski: Individual Truth

Constantin Stanislavski developed a practice centred on psychological realism: the performer finds the inner motivation of the character, builds a belief in the character’s past, and allows genuine emotion to surface through that interior work. Where Brecht wanted the audience to think, Stanislavski wanted them to feel. A Stanislavskian approach to Rani asks the performer to develop a full interior life for the character: her memories of home, her relationships before the voyage, her private fear and her private determination. None of this is stated in the text; it is held internally and filters through every choice the performer makes.

Gupta’s play needs Stanislavski most where it needs the audience to care deeply about a specific person rather than a historical category. If Rani is only the political argument — the symbol of the abandoned ayah — the play risks becoming a lecture. It is the specificity of her individual responses (her particular humour in the Lascar lodging house, her particular stubbornness in refusing to perform gratitude to Mrs Wormwood) that makes the political argument land emotionally. The Stanislavskian craft of the performer creates the individual life; the Brechtian structure of the play places that individual life within a historical argument.

Students sometimes argue that because Brecht rejected Stanislavski, no play can use both. This is historically and practically wrong. Brecht’s theoretical objection was to emotional indulgence that stopped the audience thinking; in practice, his own productions used deeply specific, truthful performers. In The Empress and in many contemporary productions of historically engaged plays, the two approaches operate at different levels: Brecht shapes the structure (how scenes are framed for the audience, what songs and direct address do) while Stanislavski shapes the individual performance (what this specific character wants in this specific moment). A strong answer holds both without collapsing them.

Design as Political Comment

A Brechtian design approach for The Empress would resist visual illusion in favour of theatrical visibility. Rather than a realistic Victorian dock, a Brechtian designer might use a stylised set: bare stage with a few key props that acquire symbolic weight (a single piece of rope, a single crate, a single chair that becomes both a dock bench and a throne depending on who sits in it and where). The lighting rig would be visible — not hidden in the flies — reminding the audience that they are in a theatre making meaning together. Projection might be used to display historical captions: “London, 1887” or “There were over 100 ayahs stranded in London each year” — Brechtian titles that comment on the scene rather than delivering it.

Costume in a Brechtian production might use a deliberately non-naturalistic approach for the multi-roled British court figures while keeping the Indian characters’ costumes specific and individually realised — a visual argument that the Empire’s functionaries are interchangeable while the Indian characters it categorises are distinct people. The blocking of the ensemble in court scenes might be semi-choreographed, almost mechanical, contrasting with the organic, varied blocking of the scenes in the Ayahs’ Home — proxemics deployed as a consistent design language throughout.

Key Fact

The best practitioner answers for The Empress do not simply apply Brecht or Stanislavski separately — they show where the two approaches operate at different levels of the same production, and why Gupta’s project of bringing hidden histories to the stage requires both the Brechtian witness-frame and the Stanislavskian individual life.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most common error in practitioner questions is describing a practitioner’s biography and then adding “this can be seen in The Empress” without explaining how. The examiner needs: the specific technique named, the specific moment of the play it applies to, the specific staging choice it produces, and the effect on the audience. A Mastering answer for a Brechtian question might read: “Brecht’s alienation effect, achieved through direct address, could be applied to Rani’s opening at Tilbury Docks: the performer steps downstage, the lighting shifts from the naturalistic dock wash to a single front-of-house profile spot, she addresses the audience directly — this creates critical distance, positioning the audience as witnesses to an injustice rather than simply spectators of a scene.” For an 8-mark performer question, use both a vocal and a physical choice so that you fully address the task.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Brecht’s epic theatre techniques — direct address, songs as interruption, gestus, ensemble multi-roling — shape the structure of The Empress, positioning the audience as witnesses to hidden history rather than emotional participants.
  • Stanislavski’s approach to interior life and individual truth is needed for the main characters, particularly Rani and Abdul — without psychological specificity the political argument risks becoming abstract.
  • A Brechtian design would use stylised, visible theatricality (bare set, visible rig, historical captions) while keeping the Indian characters’ costumes individually specific — a visual argument about who the Empire sees as a person and who it treats as a type.
