practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification that gestus is a stylised physical stance exposing social role (1); description of a specific gestural choice for the court figures (e.g. synchronised backward lean, collective turning of backs) (1); explanation that the choreographic quality makes the court read as a social institution rather than individual characters (1); link to the Brechtian purpose of making structural power visible to the audience (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Rani in the scene when she first delivers a direct address to the audience, explain how you would use vocal and physical choices to create a Brechtian witness moment rather than a naturalistic scene. Refer to a specific vocal choice and a specific physical choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band: At least one specific vocal choice in the Brechtian mode (e.g. slightly elevated, clear projection directly out to the audience, slowing pace to allow the audience to process rather than be swept along, no emotional quaver — the voice of a witness, not a victim) and at least one specific physical choice (e.g. stepping downstage centre to break the tableau of the dock scene, turning squarely to face the audience, arms at sides rather than in narrative gesture, eye contact sweeping the auditorium rather than locking to one person), both anchored to the direct address moment, both justified with reference to the Brechtian distancing effect and what it communicates to the audience; sustained.

Upper-mid band: One vocal and one physical choice, both generally specific and anchored to the moment; Brechtian intent addressed; mostly coherent.

Lower-mid band: Choices offered but without the Brechtian frame; may describe the scene naturalistically rather than as a witness address; limited reference to practitioner technique.

Low band: Emotion described rather than vocal/physical choices; no reference to practitioner technique; descriptive.

practice_questions.text: As a designer working on a production of The Empress that draws on Brechtian staging principles, explain how you would design the set and lighting for the Tilbury Docks scene to make visible the historical and political context of Rani's situation. Refer to specific design choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band: Specific Brechtian set choices (bare stage, minimal symbolic props named with their symbolic function, visible lighting rig, possible use of projected captions with historical context) and lighting choices (cool, even wash rather than atmospheric special, visible lanterns, no attempt at naturalistic illusion), each justified with reference to the Brechtian principle of theatrical visibility and the audience's role as critical witness; named moment anchored; audience effect articulated; sustained.

Upper-mid band: Set and lighting choices with some Brechtian rationale; generally specific; audience effect addressed; mostly coherent.

Lower-mid band: Design choices described but without Brechtian framing; some relevant content but limited reference to practitioner technique or audience effect.

Low band: General design ideas listed; no reference to Brechtian principles; descriptive.

practice_questions.text: You are the director of a GCSE production of The Empress. Discuss how you would use Brechtian techniques at the structural level of the production and Stanislavskian performance at the individual character level to communicate both the historical argument and the personal truth of Rani's story. Refer to at least two staging choices and at least one named performance moment.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band: Clear articulation of the two practitioners operating at different levels (Brecht: structure, framing, audience address, design visibility; Stanislavski: individual performer truth, inner motivation, psychological specificity); at least two specific staging choices that demonstrate Brechtian technique (named design element, direct address moment staged with specific lighting and physical performance choice); at least one named Stanislavskian performance moment (specific vocal and physical choice rooted in Rani's inner life at a named scene); both approaches integrated into a coherent directorial vision that justifies why the play needs both; audience effect articulated throughout; sustained.

Upper-mid band: Both practitioners addressed with some specificity; at least one staging choice and one performance moment named; mostly coherent integration of the two approaches.

Lower-mid band: Practitioners described separately without integration; some staging and performance content but limited specificity or justification.

Low band: Brief mention of Brecht and/or Stanislavski without application to specific staging choices; descriptive.

knowledge_checks.q: What term describes the Brechtian effect that creates critical distance between the audience and the performance, preventing emotional immersion?
Stanislavski's approach to performance is based on which of the following principles?
options: Performers should remain emotionally detached to allow the audience to think
Physical choreography should be more important than interior motivation
Songs and captions should interrupt the action to create political reflection
Performers should develop an inner life and emotional truth for their characters

knowledge_checks.q: A Brechtian design for The Empress might leave the lighting rig _____ to the audience, reminding them they are in a theatre.
When the British court figures are given identical, semi-choreographed gestures, this Brechtian choice uses the concept of _____.
Match each practitioner to their key contribution to a production of The Empress:
right: Shapes the structural framing — direct address, songs, visible theatricality, audience as witness
Shapes the individual performances — inner motivation, emotional truth, psychological specificity for Rani and Abdul
Influenced the original RSC production through ensemble multi-roling, music underscore and physical storytelling

glossary_terms.definition: German playwright and director (1898-1956) who developed epic theatre, arguing theatre should make audiences think critically rather than just feel.
A mode of theatre developed by Brecht that presents history as changeable and uses distancing techniques to engage the audience intellectually.
A Brechtian technique that creates critical distance between audience and performance, preventing emotional immersion.
A physical attitude that simultaneously reveals a character's social position and the playwright's political comment on that position.
Russian director (1863-1938) who developed actor training based on emotional truth, inner motivation and belief in the fictional world.
When a performer speaks to the audience rather than to another character, temporarily stepping outside the fictional world.
A staging approach using openly theatrical conventions rather than realistic illusion, inviting the audience to acknowledge the performance as constructed.
One performer playing more than one character within the same production, often used to signal that all social roles are constructed.
The planned arrangement of performer movement through the stage space, designed to create meaning and guide audience focus.
The spatial distance between performers on stage, communicating power, intimacy, tension or status.
